Structural Ingenuity

Making Stanford’s complex patient towers a reality

Stanford’s vision called for four patient towers cantilevered nearly 30 feet beyond their supporting columns, creating demanding structural and vibration challenges.

NYA had to carefully balance the weight of the projecting floors, control vibration, and integrate the towers with the hospital’s seismic system. Through advanced analysis and engineering judgment, NYA developed a multi-story steel framing solution that met these competing demands.

For Stanford, the result was the realization of its ambitious vision, without compromise.

Architectural Vision

Engineering Stanford’s vision for a brighter, more welcoming hospital.

Stanford’s atrium welcomes patients and families with daylight and open space. To achieve the nearly 120-foot skylight without bulky framing or columns, NYA designed a shallow grid of slender steel pipes. Advanced analysis allowed NYA to keep the structure light while meeting demanding engineering requirements, delivering the openness Stanford envisioned.

Seismic Leadership

Helping Stanford keep caring for patients after an earthquake

NYA drew on its pioneering seismic isolation expertise to design a system that supports Stanford’s goal of uninterrupted care. By reducing shaking within the hospital, the system helps protect patients, staff, and medical equipment. NYA’s technical expertise brought that protection into the design, reducing the risk of damage and disruption.

Site Ingenuity

Engineering a nearly million-square-foot hospital on a very small site

UCSF envisioned a major new hospital on a steep, triangular site surrounded by existing buildings, roads, and underground utilities. The limited footprint left little room for the large, flexible floors essential to modern healthcare.

NYA engineered a way to make every square foot count. Dramatic cantilevers extended usable floors beyond their supporting columns, while an innovative structural system accommodated shifting floorplates as the tower rose. Together, these solutions maximized the space available within the site’s restrictive geometry.

The result was a structural design that made UCSF’s nearly million-square-foot hospital possible on a site that seemed far too small to accommodate it.

Architectural Freedom

Making UCSF’s bold architecture possible through innovative seismic design

UCSF needed to fit an architecturally ambitious hospital onto a severely constrained site while meeting California’s demanding seismic requirements. Conventional seismic systems would have occupied precious space and imposed significant restrictions on the building’s design.

NYA engineered an innovative system combining steel moment frames with nearly 200 fluid viscous dampers. By dissipating earthquake energy without relying on restrictive walls or bracing, the system accommodated the building’s dramatic geometry and preserved its open, flexible spaces.

The result was a hospital designed for powerful earthquakes, with the architectural freedom and usable space UCSF envisioned.

Collaboration

Helping UCSF build more efficiently through two California hospital firsts

UCSF saw an opportunity to simplify construction through prefabricated MEP racks and bathroom pods. But making these innovations work required multiple engineering disciplines to resolve competing requirements before construction.

NYA brought the MEP teams together to coordinate shared racks and engineered the structural supports needed to accommodate them. This coordination also minimized MEP clashes before construction. NYA also coordinated the building structure to receive prefabricated bathroom pods.

The result was two California hospital firsts, making installation more efficient, reducing rework, and lowering construction costs for UCSF.

Advanced Rapid Concept Studies (ARCS)

Better informed structural
decisions lead to lower
construction costs

NYA’s Advanced Rapid Concept Studies (ARCS) delivers Design Development-level analysis during the earliest stages of design. By rapidly evaluating multiple structural systems with advanced seismic analysis, material quantities, and cost input, our team identifies opportunities to eliminate unnecessary steel and concrete, reduce risk, and help you select the right system with greater confidence.

Conceptual illustration of anticipated structural cost ranges.

Rapid Evaluation

Compare options with confidence

We quickly develop and analyze multiple structural systems such as moment frames, braced frames, dampers, and base isolation so you can make informed decisions before designs become difficult and expensive to change.

Advanced Analysis

DD-level detail in SD

Using nonlinear seismic analysis and our in-house computational capability, ARCS delivers a level of performance, quantities, and cost information typically reserved for later phases, giving you reliable data when system selection is most important.

Real-World Experience

Proven on complex hospitals

We have applied ARCS on major hospital projects including UCSF Helen Diller Hospital and Stanford, evaluating multiple systems with cost input and clear pros and cons. Our depth of experience with base isolation, viscous dampers, and complex hybrid systems enables solutions others cannot deliver as quickly.

Soil-Structure Interaction (SSI)

NYA’s comprehensive SSI analysis reveals
savings conventional methods miss

Typical Industry Approach

Basic SSI

Simplified, low-resolution models of soil behavior

Often results in overly conservative earthquake forces

Requires more steel, concrete, and foundation construction than necessary

The NYA Approach

NYA’s Comprehensive SSI

Sophisticated, high-resolution model of how soil behaves during an earthquake

Reveals savings that simpler models miss, allowing for a more efficient structural design

Led by world leading expert, Professor Gazetas, responsible for pioneering the field

Measured Project Value

At UCSF,
the savings went
beyond SSI.

Concern about HCAI approval often leads teams to follow conventional requirements without questioning whether a better solution exists. NYA looks deeper at the safety goals those requirements serve. Working with HCAI, we develop and substantiate alternative means of compliance that achieve those goals with less material, simpler construction, and lower cost.

One approved AMC
$2M+

Steel-cost savings from a single alternative means of compliance.

UCSF's sustainability goals prompted NYA to investigate how using less steel could lower the hospital's embodied carbon while meeting HCAI's safety requirements. We developed and secured approval for an alternative means of compliance that reduced steel quantities, advancing UCSF's low-carbon goals and saving more than $2 million in steel costs.

Project proof points reflect NYA's documented UCSF project experience and technical analysis.
1
Material savings

Reduced seismic base shear, higher-strength steel and reinforcement, and targeted structural optimization.

2
Testing + inspection

Alternative ultrasonic-testing procedures and strategic reuse of applicable damper test results.

3
Steel fabrication efficiency

Alternative box-column splices, continuity-plate details, bolted SidePlate connections, and prefabrication strategies.

4
Sustainability

Low-carbon concrete and thermal-control strategies tied to practical project delivery.

5
Constructability

Concrete-placement tolerance and other field-focused alternatives designed around how the hospital is actually built.

UC Irvine Douglas Hospital

The collaboration that helped UCI
finish on time and within budget

At UC Irvine Douglas Hospital, NYA helped align design, permitting, and construction around a then-novel phased review strategy. By separating early packages from later design work, the team secured permits for site preparation and the structure 12–18 months earlier. Coordinating these review packages with designers, builders, and regulators allowed construction to advance while more complex portions of the hospital were still being refined.

12–18
months
earlier

An exceptional outcome for UCI

UCI Douglas Hospital became the first California hospital of its era to achieve both. The approach helped establish the incremental plan-review process later used on California hospital projects.
